analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder for investors to recover money when a stock prospectus misled them.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a vote, with no cosponsors and no action after its May 1995 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Securities Act of 1933, an investor who bought a stock based on false or misleading statements in the offering prospectus can sue to undo the sale. This bill would let the company or seller escape that remedy entirely if it can show the stock's price drop came from something other than the misstatement, and would cap any damages at only the slice of the loss the seller cannot pin on other causes. In practice, that shifts much of the burden of proving what caused a loss onto the misled investor.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies selling securities, underwriters, and brokers who face lawsuits from investors who were given misleading prospectuses. They would escape full liability whenever they can point to any other plausible reason a stock lost value — a market downturn, industry news, anything — and investors would have to untangle those causes in court.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would bar the rescission remedy — unwinding the sale — whenever the defendant proves the security's depreciation came from something other than a misrepresentation or omission in the prospectus.
It would limit an investor's damages to only the portion of the loss the defendant fails to prove resulted from other causes, placing the burden of sorting out loss causation largely on the buyer.
Sen. Bennett introduced the bill as the 'Securities Act Amendment of 1995,' amending Section 12(2) of the Securities Act of 1933.

analysis.who_pays: Investors who rely on offering documents. When a company's prospectus misleads them, they would recover less — or nothing — even where the misstatement was material, because the seller gets a path to deflect blame for the price drop onto unrelated causes.

drawbacks.text: Defendants could argue that stock-price drops reflected market conditions or other causes rather than the misstatement, and legitimate claims tied to genuine market losses would be filtered out, reducing litigation against honest issuers.

The cost to honest supporters: investors defrauded by misstatements would bear the cost of proving exactly how much of their loss the fraud caused — often the hardest fact question in the case — and some victims of real misstatements would recover nothing at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is one-sided: it hands securities sellers a strong escape hatch from prospectus liability while giving investors a harder, costlier road to recovery. Any benefit from reduced litigation against sellers comes directly out of the pockets of misled buyers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and the 104th Congress ended without the bill ever coming to a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Bennett introduced the Securities Act Amendment of 1995 on May 25, 1995, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action appears in the record — the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or a cosponsor.
The Congress ended on January 3, 1997, so the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investors, who kept the full prospectus-liability remedy the bill would have narrowed; the bill's death meant sellers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Robert F. Bennett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 25, 1995; it was his only action of record on it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action; it never got a markup or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted no cosponsors and never reached a vote, so no partisan pattern on its merits appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would shield sellers of securities from full liability for misleading prospectuses, letting them shift blame for a stock's decline onto other causes. The gain comes directly at the expense of investors suing over those misstatements.
Buyers of securities relying on offering documents would recover less when misled: rescission could be barred and damages capped at the portion of the loss the defendant cannot explain away.
